forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Raise from 30% to 32% (CI [17,44] to [18,48]). The 11-12 August window itself was quiet on AGI-relevant capability news; the move is driven by an on-point market reading the prior did not appear to price, not by fresh headlines. Dated items actually in the window: (1) Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard re-stamped 11 Aug 2026, combined median AGI year 2031, 80% interval 2027-2043 - identical to the 10 Aug reading, so no drift. (2) Sundar Pichai's Google DeepMind reorganisation (announced 5 Aug, restated in 11 Aug coverage) confirming Demis Hassabis as Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet explicitly to focus on AGI; Hassabis told staff AGI 'is close at hand'. Rhetoric, not an announcement. (3) 11 Aug: Riot Platforms disclosed a 20-year, $9.1bn / ~191MW compute agreement with Anthropic phased through 2027-28; NVIDIA assembled a >$500bn AI-infrastructure financing alliance (WSJ); Anthropic scrapped its planned Sonnet 5 price rise; OpenAI's only dedicated ethicist Chloe Bakalar departed (FT). None bear on AGI declaration. (4) AI-Weekly issue 229 (11 Aug) contains no post-10 Aug AGI item. Nothing dated 12 Aug is relevant; Google's 12 Aug event is Pixel 11 hardware. TRIGGER CHECK. UP triggers: NOOA/ARC-AGI-3 above 60% on the ARC Prize verified leaderboard DID NOT FIRE, and moved against - ARC Prize's own verified board still shows Claude Opus 5 at 30.16% (verified 24 Jul 2026) and GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.78%, while NVIDIA's 85.1% RHAE and Impossible Research's 'Schema' ~99% RHAE are explicitly self-reported and unverified, and OpenAI's competing 38.3% for Sol requires non-standard Responses-API settings. Astra shipping DID NOT FIRE - still unshipped, with Axios (7 Aug) reporting OpenAI slowing release over possible 'Critical' cyber capability. 2+ leading researchers stating AGI achieved DID NOT FIRE in-window. EO 14409 abandonment DID NOT FIRE - the framework lapsed its 1 Aug deadline but was briefed to industry on 4 Aug, voluntary and excluding open-weight models. DOWN triggers: mandatory pre-release review DID NOT FIRE; aggregate median drifting later DID NOT FIRE. What did change the view: Kalshi's on-point series KXAGICO ('Will any company announce it has achieved AGI before 1 Jan 2030?') reads last price $0.76, bid 68c / ask 79c, open interest ~2,264, 24h volume zero, last updated 9 Apr 2026. That is far above 30% and matches an announcement-style resolution rather than a capability-style one. It is thin, stale, and the sibling ladder is non-monotonic (Jan-2028 53% vs Apr-2028 50%), so it carries light weight - but it justifies a 2pp nudge and a materially fatter right tail rather than a pure hold.
forecasts.base_rate: Two distinguishable reference classes bear on this question and they disagree sharply. Class A is capability-based AGI-arrival forecasting: the Goodheart Labs aggregator (Metaculus, Manifold, Kalshi Turing-test market), stamped 11 Aug 2026, gives median 2031 with an 80% interval of 2027-2043. Interpolating a right-skewed CDF with a 2027 tenth percentile and 2031 median puts P(arrival before 1 Jan 2030) at roughly 30-35%. Metaculus Q5121 ('first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced') is later still at around January 2033 (interquartile roughly 2029-2040), and the Metaculus community has pushed timelines out, not in, from 2025 to 2026. Class B is announcement-based prediction markets, which match this question's resolution wording much more closely. Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP-29 asks precisely whether any verifiable company announces it has achieved AGI before 1 Jan 2030 and last traded at 76c (68/79 bid-ask). Sibling strikes read roughly 71c for before-2029 and 81c for before-2031. Sample size is the limitation: KXAGICO has only ~3,500 contracts of lifetime volume, ~2,300 open interest and zero 24-hour volume, with the last price stamped 9 April 2026 - almost certainly a stale mark set around Sam Altman's April 2026 podcast claim that 'AGI is something we've already reached without noticing', and Jensen Huang's March 2026 'I think we've achieved AGI'. That neither statement resolved this question implies the resolver applies a stricter bar (an official lab announcement, or three named researchers) than Kalshi's loose 'company officially announces' wording. That argues for anchoring nearer Class A while allowing a fat upper tail for a declaration event. A further structural consideration pulls up: OpenAI's October 2025 Microsoft agreement ends its 15%-of-revenue obligation on 'AGI achieved or 2032', giving one leading lab a direct financial incentive to declare. Overall: ~30% from Class A, ~70% from a heavily discounted Class B, blended toward Class A at roughly one-third weight.

factors_up.factor: Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP-29 (any company announces AGI before 1 Jan 2030) marked at 76c, bid 68 / ask 79, directly on-point with an announcement-style resolution (read 12 Aug 2026)
Standing declaration incentive: OpenAI's 15% revenue share to Microsoft terminates on 'AGI achieved or 2032'; Altman already floated 'let's agree we've attained AGI' (Apr 2026)
Hassabis elevated to Alphabet Chief Scientist explicitly to focus on AGI, saying it 'is close at hand' (announced 5 Aug, restated in 11 Aug Pichai coverage)
Compute build-out continues at scale - Riot/Anthropic $9.1bn 191MW deal and NVIDIA's $500bn financing alliance, both 11 Aug 2026

factors_down.factor: ARC Prize verified leaderboard still tops out at Claude Opus 5 30.16% (verified 24 Jul 2026); NVIDIA NOOA 85.1% and Schema ~99% remain self-reported and explicitly unverified
Aggregate median AGI year unchanged at 2031 on the 11 Aug 2026 Goodheart stamp - still after the deadline; Metaculus Q5121 later still at ~2033
Astra remains unshipped with no model card or pricing; OpenAI slowing release over possible Critical cyber tier (Axios, 7 Aug 2026) - shipping friction, not capability proof
Two prominent 'AGI achieved' claims already exist (Huang Mar 2026, Altman Apr 2026) without resolving this question, evidencing a strict resolution bar

key_uncertainties: Resolution ambiguity: whether a CEO podcast declaration (Altman, Apr 2026) or a chip-vendor CEO claim (Huang, Mar 2026) counts as 'a credible AI lab publicly announces AGI' - the prior implies not, but the margin is thin
Whether the Kalshi 76c mark reflects a real belief or is a stale April artefact with zero 24-hour volume and an 11-point bid-ask spread
Whether harness-driven ARC-AGI-3 gains (NOOA, Schema) reflect genuine generality or benchmark-specific scaffolding; ARC Prize does not verify by default
Astra's true capability profile, still unobservable outside OpenAI's own maths and cyber claims
Whether commercial incentives (Microsoft revenue share, IPO positioning for both OpenAI and Anthropic in H2 2026) trigger a definitional AGI declaration well before capability consensus
update_triggers: Revise UP if OpenAI, Google DeepMind or Anthropic issues an official corporate statement (not a podcast remark) that it has achieved AGI, or if 3+ named leading researchers say so within a short window
Revise UP if ARC Prize verifies any harness or model above 60% on ARC-AGI-3 under its own protocol, or if Astra ships with a model card showing broad frontier generality
Revise UP if KXAGICO-COMP-29 trades with real volume and holds above 70c, or if the Goodheart combined median moves to 2029 or earlier
Revise DOWN if the Goodheart combined median drifts to 2032 or later, or Metaculus Q3479/Q5121 push out further

Revise DOWN if NOOA or Schema results fail replication under ARC's protocol, if Astra is released and shows weak out-of-domain generality, or if the EO 14409 voluntary framework hardens into mandatory pre-release review that delays frontier launches

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Small DOWN move: central 20% to 19%, CI [10,33] to [10,32]. Three dated items in the 11-12 August window, all pointing mildly against a rapid AI-driven collapse of the sector, and no UP trigger fired. (1) 12 Aug 2026, Consultancy.uk: PwC became the fourth Big Four firm caught publishing AI-generated thought leadership. GPTZero put an 84% probability that PwC Middle East's 'Transforming Governance' was entirely generative text, and found no public evidence for the 'Citizen Pulse' government deployments it claimed in Denmark, Saudi Arabia, the US and Australia. This completes a set: Deloitte refunded AU$440,000 to Australia's Department of Employment and Workplace Relations over fabricated citations; GPTZero found 40 of 45 sources hallucinated in KPMG's October 2025 agentic-AI report; and in May 2026 EY Canada's loyalty-fraud report was alleged to be 72% AI-generated with 16 of 27 citations broken or non-existent. This is genuinely double-edged. It is direct evidence that firms are substituting AI for human production, which deflates revenue per head. But it is stronger evidence for the reason the resolution bar is hard to clear: the failure mode is exactly the accountability-and-verification layer clients pay for, and the reputational cost is being borne by the firms, not passed to clients as savings. Matt Parry (The Future Collective), quoted 12 Aug, notes hallucinations get scraped back into models with no retraction mechanism, which raises rather than lowers the value of humanly-warranted analysis. (2) 12 Aug 2026, Consultancy.uk: Cornerstone Research, a pure-play economic and financial consultancy with over 1,000 professionals across nine US/UK/EU offices, named Bryan Ricchetti CEO. His stated agenda is to 'continue to invest in outstanding talent' alongside AI capabilities. Expansion posture, not retrenchment, in the exact sub-sector the question targets. (3) 11 Aug 2026, Consultancy.uk: a majority of C-suite executives say AI adoption is 'tearing their company apart' and eight in ten organisations are struggling with adoption despite record investment; CreateFuture's Lindsay Ratcliffe describes firms approaching a value 'cliff edge'. Adoption friction is the consultant's market. Adjacent and very recent but not strictly in-window: CRA International reported Q2 2026 revenue of $210.8m, its highest quarter ever, up 12.8% year on year, raised FY26 guidance to $805-820m, and returned to 3.3% net headcount growth. TRIGGER CHECK: no UP trigger fired. No Big 4 or MBB double-digit AI-attributed revenue decline; no 15% client-facing headcount fall; no BLS or ONS print showing a 10% sector fall (BLS management/scientific/technical consulting remains above 1.4m and is projected to grow 9.4% 2024-34); and no credible analysis approaching a 33% AI-attributed contraction. DOWN triggers are not yet formally testable, but CRA's record H1 is partial support.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: professional-services sectors losing 33%+ of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with the loss primarily attributed to a single technology by multiple credible analyses. The class is small and every member is imperfect. US travel agencies lost roughly 40-50% of employment 1995-2010, but over fifteen years and via pure disintermediation of a transactional function. Legal document review contracted sharply after 2010 with predictive coding, but that is a task inside a sector, not a sector. Typesetting and commercial printing collapsed over two decades. Bank tellers, often cited, did not fall 33% in six years. Stock photography and travel are the closest fast cases, and both involved a product that was fully digital and unbundled from relationship, accountability and implementation. Advisory work is a bundle: analysis, relationship capital, political cover, transfer of blame, regulatory credentialing and delivery capacity. Only the analysis layer is directly automatable, and it is a minority of the fee. That drives a base rate of roughly 5-12% for a six-year 33% decline. Adjust upward for the AI capability trajectory, documented graduate-intake cuts (KPMG UK graduate class down 29%, Deloitte down 18%, EY down 11%, PwC down 6%), three consecutive starting-salary freezes at McKinsey and BCG, McKinsey's headcount decline from 49,840 in 2023 to 44,969 in 2026, and Accenture's Q3 FY26 bookings down 2%. Adjust downward for the double resolution bar: the 33% magnitude AND primary AI attribution certified by two or more credible analyses. Attribution is the harder half, because macro demand, post-pandemic normalisation and audit-market pressure are competing explanations any careful analyst will foreground. Sample size is effectively n<5, so the base rate carries wide uncertainty and is not treated as precise.

factors_up.factor: 12 Aug 2026 (Consultancy.uk): all four Big Four now caught passing off AI-generated thought leadership, confirming firms are already substituting AI for human production in lead-generating work
Entry-level pipeline compression persists: KPMG UK graduate class cut 29%, Deloitte 18%, EY 11%, PwC 6%; McKinsey and BCG froze starting salaries for a third year running
Accenture Q3 FY26 new bookings down 2% year on year and shares down over 50% across twelve months on client-insourcing fears, showing the market prices genuine fee-pool compression
McKinsey headcount down from 49,840 (2023) to 44,969 (2026), with roughly 10% cuts planned in non-client-facing functions over 18-24 months

factors_down.factor: 12 Aug 2026: Cornerstone Research, a 1,000-plus person pure-play economic consultancy, names a new CEO on an explicit talent-investment and expansion agenda, with no retrenchment signal
11 Aug 2026: a majority of C-suite say AI adoption is tearing their company apart and eight in ten organisations struggle to realise value, sustaining demand for external advice
CRA International reported record Q2 2026 revenue of $210.8m (up 12.8% y/y) in early Aug 2026, raised FY26 guidance to $805-820m and returned to 3.3% headcount growth
Source Global Research forecasts tech consulting to pass $400bn globally in 2026 at 7% growth; MCA projects UK sector growth of 5.7% in 2026 and 7.4% in 2027, driven by AI mandates
The AI hallucination scandals reinforce that clients buy verified accountability, not text, which is the part of the bundle least exposed to automation

key_uncertainties: Whether AI-driven cuts move from support and audit functions into client-facing consultant headcount; to date the evidence is almost entirely back-office and graduate intake
Whether the resolution's attribution bar can ever be met, since macro demand, post-pandemic normalisation and audit-market pressure will always be competing explanations

Whether 'economic consultancy' is scoped narrowly (pure-play economic consultancies such as CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Frontier, where revenue is currently at record levels) or broadly to include Big 4 advisory and IT consulting, which changes the answer materially
Whether client insourcing of analysis using their own AI stacks accelerates, which is the single mechanism that could compress the fee pool fast rather than gradually
Whether revenue holds while headcount falls, in which case a 33% employment decline could resolve YES even with flat or growing revenue
update_triggers: Revise UP if any Big 4 or MBB firm reports an annual revenue decline above 10% attributed primarily to AI

Revise UP if client-facing consultant headcount at two or more major firms falls more than 15% in a single year, or if a pure-play economic consultancy (CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Frontier) reports a revenue decline
Revise UP if BLS management/scientific/technical consulting employment or ONS UK professional services employment falls more than 10% from the 2024 baseline
Revise UP if Source Global Research, Kennedy or a peer-reviewed study publishes an AI-attributed sector contraction estimate approaching 33%
Revise DOWN if full-year 2026 sector revenue growth is positive across Big 4 and MBB, or if UK/US graduate intake recovers toward 2024 levels in the 2027 cycle
Revise DOWN if the AI thought-leadership scandals produce documented client demand for human-certified deliverables, or if firms begin charging an explicit assurance premium

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 52 to 54 (+2pp). CI shifts from [37,65] to [39,66], with a marginal narrowing. The single genuinely new item in the 11-12 August window is a YouGov Westminster voting intention poll published 11 August 2026 (fieldwork 9-10 August, for The Times and Sky News): Labour 24 (+2), Reform UK 22 (-1), Conservatives 21 (+2), Greens 12 (-1), Lib Dems 11 (-1), Restore Britain 4, SNP 3, Plaid 2. This matters more than its 2pp margin suggests. The prior explicitly flagged YouGov as a house showing Reform ahead and possibly not updated post-handover; YouGov had Ref 23 / Lab 22 on 2-3 August, Ref 22 / Lab 22 on 26-27 July, and Ref 23 / Lab 21 on 22-23 July. YouGov itself notes this is Labour's highest in its tracker since July 2025, up eight points from a 16% low in May, and that Reform's 22 is the joint-lowest since YouGov restarted VI polling in January 2025. Greens at 12 are nine points off their February peak, which cuts against the prior's Green-flank-loss worry. Second, coverage on 11 August (HuffPost, The London Economic, GB News, Left Foot Forward) amplified a Lord Ashcroft poll showing Lab 27, Con 23, Ref 18 - Reform third. Ashcroft's own write-up appears dated 8 August, so it is treated as borderline-new rather than in-window and discounted accordingly. Aggregators disagree, which is the honest disconfirming point: PollCheck's 7-poll average (10 August) has Lab 25.7 / Ref 23.4 / Con 20.6; UK Fact Check (11 August) has Lab 27 / Ref 24; but PolitPro's trend (11 August) still has Reform marginally ahead at 24.4 to Labour's 24.0. TRIGGER CHECK: none fired cleanly. UP trigger 1 (Labour lead above 3pp sustained four weeks, multiple houses) DID NOT FIRE - the lead is roughly 2-3pp, roughly three weeks old (Labour first led around 24 July), and one aggregator still shows Reform ahead. UP trigger 2 (post-handover YouGov or Stonehaven MRP flipping to Labour largest) DID NOT FIRE - no new GB-wide MRP was published in the window; MRP evidence remains dispersed and mostly stale. UP trigger 3 DID NOT FIRE - the Met Section 61 PPERA inquiry into Fiona Cottrell's donations has two people interviewed and no arrests, and the Standards Commissioner has issued no Harborne ruling. DOWN triggers: Reform has not regained a lead; no Budget gilt selloff (10-year gilt around 4.92-4.95% on 10 August, below July's 5.04% peak); Burnham's net approval is +16 on Opinium, the only positive leader rating; Clacton votes 13 August so its trigger cannot yet fire.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class remains parties narrowly ahead in national polls roughly 3-3.5 years before a UK general election. Since 1945 there are only around 15-18 usable mid-term observations, and roughly half to three-fifths of narrow leaders at this horizon go on to win most seats. That small sample is the binding limitation: it is drawn almost entirely from a two-party system, whereas current polling shows five blocs within about 15 points of each other (PollCheck 10 August: Lab 25.7, Ref 23.4, Con 20.6, Grn 12.0, LD 9.7). Under FPTP with five competitive blocs, seat outcomes are hypersensitive to small vote moves, so vote-share leads translate into seat leads far less reliably than the historical base rate assumes. This argues for keeping the central estimate close to the base rate and the interval wide, rather than reading a 2-3pp lead as decisive. A second correction runs the other way: incumbent honeymoons after a mid-term leadership handover typically decay. Burnham became PM in July 2026; Lord Ashcroft's 8 August analysis explicitly frames the bounce as real but conditional - voters are already asking how the promises will be paid for. The 28 October Budget is the obvious decay point. MRP evidence is unhelpfully dispersed and mostly stale: projections found range from Labour 144 seats (an older Reform-favourable model) to Labour 290-320, with PollCheck's demographic model at Labour 269 as largest and PLMR's July MRP at Labour 217 as largest. Averaging these is not meaningful given different vintages and methods; the honest reading is that several current-vintage models put Labour largest while the Reform-largest models predate the handover. Net: the base rate plus the fragmentation penalty plus honeymoon decay supports a central figure only modestly above 50, which is where 54 sits.

factors_up.factor: YouGov VI published 11 Aug 2026 (fieldwork 9-10 Aug) flips to Lab 24 / Ref 22 / Con 21, Labour's best since July 2025 and Reform's joint-lowest since Jan 2025 - a house that had shown Reform ahead now converges with the rest
Greens at 12 in YouGov (11 Aug), down nine points from their February peak, directly weakening the prior's Green-flank-loss concern
Burnham net approval +16 on Opinium as of early August, the only party leader with positive net approval; Ipsos (fieldwork 30 Jul-4 Aug) has him preferred as PM over Farage and Badenoch
Reform under sustained financing pressure - Met Section 61 PPERA inquiry into two £250,000 Cottrell donations ongoing, plus the unresolved Harborne £5m standards referral

The Labour lead is roughly three weeks old (first leads around 24 July) and coincides exactly with the Burnham handover, so it is a honeymoon signal with a known decay pattern
Lord Ashcroft's 8 Aug finding that voters are already asking how Burnham's promises will be paid for, with the 28 October Budget as the test
No new GB-wide MRP in the window; Reform-largest MRPs remain unrefuted by any post-handover seat-level model

key_uncertainties: Whether the YouGov flip is signal or a single poll within margin of error - YouGov itself says all parties are within MOE of the previous wave
Whether a post-handover GB-wide MRP would show Labour largest on these vote shares, given five-bloc fragmentation makes vote-to-seat translation unstable
How much of Labour's recovery is Burnham honeymoon that decays by the 28 October Budget versus a durable re-consolidation of 2024 Labour voters
Whether Reform's decline reflects Farage financing scandals specifically (potentially reversible) or broader Farage fatigue
Whether Conservative recovery to 21-23 splits the anti-Labour right durably or eventually consolidates behind one party
update_triggers: Revise UP if Labour holds a 3pp-plus aggregate lead across four consecutive weeks with at least three houses agreeing, including PolitPro's trend flipping to Labour
Revise UP if a post-handover GB-wide MRP from YouGov, Stonehaven, More in Common or Focaldata projects Labour largest on seats
Revise UP if the Met Section 61 PPERA investigation produces arrests or charges, or the Standards Commissioner finds against Farage on the Harborne gift with a suspension recommendation
Revise DOWN if Reform regains a lead across three or more houses, or if Farage wins Clacton on 13 August on a high turnout with a share materially above the ~73% Survation implied
Revise DOWN if the 28 October Budget triggers a gilt selloff (30-year back above the July 5.75% peak) or a policy reversal, or if Burnham's net approval turns negative

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 86% to 85%, CI [72,93] to [71,93]. A near-hold with a 1pp downward nudge. Nothing in the 11-12 August window bears directly on 2035; the small move comes from partial deflation of two capability signals the prior explicitly leaned on. FIRST, the prior's headline UP trigger did not merely fail to fire, it was actively disconfirmed. ARC Prize's published testing policy states it does not verify ARC-AGI-3 submissions by default and verifies only a small number of extraordinary submissions at its discretion. The August 2026 verified snapshot still shows Claude Opus 5 at 30.2% as SOTA, verified 24 July 2026, ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8%. NVIDIA's NOOA harness claim of 85.1% mean RHAE sits on the public demo set, which commentary characterises as saturating, with held-out performance untested. So the 85.1% figure is harness engineering on a saturating public split, not a verified model-capability jump. SECOND, dated 11 August coverage reframes GPT-5.6-Cyber. Help Net Security (11 Aug) and TechTimes (11 Aug) report GPT-5.6-Cyber completing 95% of exploit-chain, auth-bypass and privilege-escalation requests versus 1.5% for guardrailed GPT-5.6 - a policy and refusal gap on the same base model, not a new capability tier. The CVE-2026-15903 V8 chain is real and patched via coordinated disclosure, but the delta is an access unlock. Both items push toward the reading that recent headline progress is scaffolding- and permission-limited rather than evidence of a step change in general capability, which is the axis this question is most sensitive to. Offsetting, capex durability strengthened. OpenAI completed a $7bn employee tender at an $852bn valuation on 11 August, with the S-1 expected on EDGAR mid-to-late August. NVIDIA's $500bn financing alliance with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR (announced 10 Aug, covered 11 Aug) creates dedicated capital pools using GPUs as collateral; Intel is tapping markets for a further $20bn (11 Aug); TSMC July sales are up 45%. Meta open-weighted Muse Glimmer and committed to opening Muse Spark 1.2 (10 Aug) - diffusion, not frontier capability. TRIGGER CHECK: UP on verified ARC-AGI-3 DID NOT FIRE and was disconfirmed. UP on autonomous AI-automated AI research DID NOT FIRE; the Karpathy AutoResearch and GPT-5.3-Codex items predate the window. UP on 2+ researchers declaring AGI DID NOT FIRE. UP on aggregate median inside 2030 DID NOT FIRE; Goodheart Labs held at median 2031 (stamped 8 Aug), 80% interval now quoted 2027-2044. DOWN on median beyond 2033 DID NOT FIRE. DOWN on capex retrenchment DID NOT FIRE; the opposite. DOWN on binding international pacing DID NOT FIRE; the UN Global Dialogue's next session is May 2027, and the OpenAI/Anthropic slowdown letter (29 July) is voluntary. DOWN on two flat frontier releases is not testable; no new frontier base model appeared in the window.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: aggregated expert and market forecasts for AGI arriving within roughly 8.5 years, cross-checked against the historical base rate for transformative technologies arriving inside a decade of confident expert prediction. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard (aggregating Metaculus, Manifold, Kalshi), stamped 8 August 2026, gives a combined median AGI year of 2031 with an 80% interval of 2027-2044. A median of 2031 against a 1 January 2035 deadline implies materially above 50%; naive log-normal interpolation on that interval puts roughly 70-78% mass before 2035. The announcement-based resolution criterion is looser than the capability-based definitions those markets use, so the question resolves on a lower bar: any credible lab declaration, or three leading researchers asserting AGI achieved. Over 8.5 years, with multiple well-capitalised labs competing on narrative and with Jensen Huang having already said in March 2026 that AGI has been achieved, the probability that some declaration clears the bar is high, which is what pushes the estimate into the mid-80s rather than the low-70s. Limitations are substantial. First, market medians for AGI have historically been unstable and directionally biased toward optimism, then corrected: the AI 2027 team moved its median from ~2027 to ~2030, and Metaculus, Dario Amodei and Peter Wildeford all lengthened timelines during 2025-2026. Metaculus's own community sits later than the aggregate at 25% by 2029 and 50% by 2033. Second, the outside view on transformative technology (fusion, full self-driving, general-purpose robotics) argues for heavy discounting of confident decade-out predictions. Third, resolution ambiguity cuts both ways: 'credible lab' and 'leading researcher' are undefined, and the definitional fog around AGI documented throughout 2026 means a resolver could reasonably reject loose declarations. That ambiguity is a bigger driver of the residual 15% than any pure capability consideration.

factors_up.factor: OpenAI completed a $7bn employee tender at an $852bn valuation on 11 Aug 2026, with the S-1 expected on EDGAR mid-to-late August - capital access for a decade-long buildout is intact

NVIDIA's $500bn financing alliance with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR (10 Aug, covered 11 Aug) converts GPU clusters into financeable infrastructure assets, extending the capex runway well past 2030

Meta open-weighting Muse Glimmer and committing to open Muse Spark 1.2 (10 Aug) broadens the number of actors who could plausibly make an AGI-class declaration by 2035

factors_down.factor: ARC Prize policy confirms ARC-AGI-3 submissions are not verified by default; verified SOTA remains Claude Opus 5 at 30.2% (24 July), so NVIDIA's 85.1% RHAE is unverified harness performance on a saturating public split

GPT-5.6-Cyber's 95% vs 1.5% task-completion gap versus guardrailed GPT-5.6 (Help Net Security and TechTimes, 11 Aug) shows the 10 Aug zero-day result was a permissions unlock on the same base model, not a capability step change

key_uncertainties: Whether current progress is scaffolding-limited or capability-limited - the 11-12 Aug evidence (harness-driven ARC-AGI-3 gains, refusal-policy-driven cyber gains) tilts toward scaffolding, but three weeks without a frontier base-model release is far too short a window to conclude anything

update_triggers: Revise UP if a frontier base model (not a harness, fine-tune or refusal-policy variant) posts a verified ARC-AGI-3 held-out score materially above 30.2%, confirming capability rather than scaffolding gains
Revise UP if the OpenAI S-1, expected on EDGAR mid-to-late August 2026, discloses revenue and gross margins that make the current capex trajectory self-funding through 2030

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD at 7%, CI unchanged at [4,12]. The hold is deliberate: genuinely new evidence appeared on 11-12 August, but it pushed the two branches of this disjunctive question in opposite directions and roughly cancelled. What did change is the internal composition of the 7% - more of it now sits on the blockade/quarantine branch and less on the amphibious-assault branch. NEW AND DATED IN WINDOW. (1) On 11 August the PRC Ministry of National Defense announced that Type 054A frigate Honghe will conduct a joint navigation, communications and at-sea-replenishment exercise with an Indonesian Navy frigate in waters EAST of Taiwan in mid-August (Bloomberg 11 Aug; Reuters 11 Aug; Taipei Times 12 Aug). Reporting states this is the first time Beijing has publicly announced training with a foreign navy in those waters. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council condemned it the same evening as a military provocation and as 'exercises in name, expansion in fact' intended to manufacture an impression of PRC jurisdiction east of Taiwan. (2) Taipei Times, 12 August: Taiwan's Maritime and Port Bureau (statement Monday 10 Aug) called China's Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration order of Thursday 6 August imposing traffic controls on northbound vessels in the Strait during Typhoon Dolphin 'unacceptable', urged vessels to disregard it, and asserted the Strait is international waters. The US State Department told CNA on Monday 10 August that it 'opposes any actions that interfere with the freedoms of navigation and overflight applicable in the Taiwan Strait' (Focus Taiwan 11 Aug; Taipei Times 11 Aug). (3) Taipei Times front page, 11 August: a Taiwanese national security official's readout of the Beidaihe meeting lists four Taiwan resolutions - oppose independence by force, strengthen 'de facto governance' via legal and cognitive warfare, mobilise united-front resources, and give all-out support to 'patriotic forces' in the November nine-in-one local elections - plus a US strategy of trade courtship and blocking a new phase of arms sales to Taiwan, ahead of Xi's 24 September US visit. TRIGGER CHECK. DID NOT FIRE: no named large-scale PLA exercise in response to Han Kuang 42 or the Ketagalan Forum (held 4 Aug) as of 12 Aug; no US-China rupture (the Beidaihe readout implies the opposite); ADIZ activity remains far below 2024-25 norms (MND daily reports: 4 sorties to 6am 9 Aug, 1 on 10 Aug, 2 on 11 Aug). FIRED PARTIALLY: the maritime traffic-control trigger was worded 'without weather pretext' - a typhoon pretext existed, so it fired only in spirit, though Taipei and Washington both treated the pretext as cover for a jurisdiction claim. UNRESOLVED: Han Kuang 42 ends 14 Aug and the ISW-AEI update (last published 7 Aug) is still pending, so both DOWN triggers remain live rather than confirmed.
forecasts.base_rate: Outside view unchanged. Primary reference class: major-power initiation of an amphibious assault or sustained naval blockade against a defended territory since 1945. This is a handful of cases in eighty years, implying an annual hazard in the low single digits and roughly 3-8% over the remaining 3.4-year window. Narrower class: Taiwan Strait crises since 1995 - the 1995-96 missile crises, the 2022 Pelosi exercises, Joint Sword 2024A and 2024B, and Strait Thunder 2025 - five to six coercive episodes, none escalating past large exercises. Zero for six, but with N that small the upper credible bound on per-crisis escalation is not far below 20%, which is why the CI extends to 12 rather than to 9. Limitations worth stating plainly. First, both reference classes are drawn from a world without the 2027 PLA capability milestone, so they may understate the tail. Second, the resolution criterion is disjunctive and asymmetric: a blockade lasting more than 72 hours is a materially lower bar than an invasion, and the coast guard and maritime-safety activity now running east of and inside the Strait sits on a continuum whose upper end could satisfy it. Third, the trend evidence is ambiguous by construction. PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan fell to 1,334 in H1 2026, more than halved year on year and a three-year low, with no large-scale named drill around the island in 2026 - the first such year since 2022 (SCMP tally of MND data). Low tempo is equally consistent with de-escalation, with internal PLA turmoil and purges, with fuel and resource conservation, and with deliberate signal suppression ahead of a shift to a coast-guard-led coercion model. The quiet air picture is not treated as strong evidence either way, and the ADIZ lull is not converted into a large downward move. Fourth, single-source anonymous readouts of Beidaihe are weak evidence, so the 11 August report carries light weight.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD at 1%, 80% CI unchanged at [0,2]. The 11-12 August window produced genuinely new evidence, but it points mildly AGAINST a sub-2.0% print, and the central estimate is already at the practical floor, so the honest update is no numeric change with a slightly firmer lower tail. NEW, DATED EVIDENCE (11-12 Aug 2026). (1) Shipping escalation. On 11-12 August, Houthi forces attacked the Tanzania-flagged Tihamah in the Bab el-Mandeb, killing three crew - reported as the first fatalities from a Houthi strike on a ship since the war began on 28 February (CNBC 12 Aug, Insurance Journal 11 Aug, Manila Times 12 Aug). Separately, the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova was hit by a missile entering the Gulf of Oman. (2) Hormuz talks at an impasse, not a deal. Despite the US targeting Wednesday 12 August for an announcement, CNBC's 11 August piece is headlined 'Hormuz deadlock... prospects for an imminent deal fade'. Iran continues to condition reopening on sanctions relief and reparations. (3) Brent back to roughly $90. Brent rose about 1.24-1.4% on 12 August to $88.91-$90.00 (CNBC 12 Aug; TradingEconomics: $89.24 on 11 Aug, +1.73%, +34.96% year-on-year). (4) A small offset: UK NBP day-ahead gas FELL 3.25% on 11 August to 144.86p/therm, unwinding part of the 10 August spike. But the level is still up about 16.7% over one month and about 82% year-on-year. (5) The House of Commons Library inflation briefing was refreshed 11 August 10:31 UTC. It confirms the last print (June CPI 2.6%) and, notably, softer underlying detail: core 2.6%, services 3.6%, food 1.7% (lowest since August 2024). No new ONS print - the next CPI release is still 19 August. Labour market is 18 August, GDP 13 August. TRIGGER CHECK: the UP trigger 'Hormuz deal signed AND Brent below $70' DID NOT FIRE - no deal, and Brent moved the wrong way. The '19 August July CPI at or below 2.2%' and 'Ofgem 26 August cap cut' triggers cannot yet fire; both releases are still ahead. 'BoE revises Q4 path below 2.5%' DID NOT FIRE - the 30 July MPR path peaks near 3.2% in Q4. The DOWN trigger 'Brent sustains above $90 with Hormuz talks collapsed' is PARTIALLY fired: Brent touched roughly $90 and talks are deadlocked, but talks have not formally collapsed and one day is not a sustained level, so it is not treated as fully met. The 'July or August CPI at or above 3.0%' and 'cap materially above £1,899' triggers are untested. One pre-existing factor the prior did not mention: VAT on domestic electricity goes to zero for six months from 1 October (announced 21 July, worth about £45 off a typical bill), a real mechanical drag of roughly 0.1pp on Q4 CPI. That is nowhere near enough to bridge a gap of over 1pp against a rising path, and it was known before 11 August.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: months in which UK annual CPI printed below 2.0%, conditional on the most recent print being 2.6% and every major official and independent forecaster projecting a rise over the following two quarters. Since the CPI series began in 1989, sub-2.0% prints are not rare in absolute terms (much of 1999-2005 and 2014-2016, plus 2020-2021 and September 2024), so the unconditional monthly base rate is roughly 30-35%. But the conditional base rate is what matters. Falling from 2.6% to below 2.0% within five reference months, against a consensus path heading to about 3.2% in Q4 (BoE MPR, 30 July 2026) and NIESR's 3.1% 2026 average, has essentially no historical precedent outside a demand collapse (2008-09, 2020) or a sharp, sustained energy price fall. Here energy is doing the opposite: NBP gas is up about 82% year-on-year and Brent is up about 35% year-on-year. Mechanically the window is tight. Only the July through November 2026 reference months can be published before 1 January 2027 (19 August through mid-December). July CPI would need a fall of more than 0.6pp in a single month with no obvious base effect and with the October price cap and the Middle East pass-through still ahead. Limitations: base rates from a 37-year series with only a handful of regime shifts are thin. The VAT-to-zero electricity cut from 1 October is a genuine policy shock the historical class does not contain, and food inflation at 1.7% plus core at 2.6% are softer than the headline narrative implies. A rapid Hormuz reopening plus an energy unwind is a real, if unlikely, path. That is why the upper CI bound stays at 2 rather than collapsing to zero, and why certainty is never stated.

The Numbers film page, retrieved live on 12 August 2026, reports: Domestic $671,028,646 (cumulative through Monday 10 August 2026, day 11); International $1,017,739,165 (territory report date 11 August 2026); Worldwide $1,688,767,811. That is $188,767,811 of headroom above the $1.5B bar, or 12.6% above the threshold. This is genuinely new relative to the 11 August prior, which carried domestic around $654M (through Sunday 9 August) and roughly $172M of headroom: the Monday 10 August daily add of $16,685,732 and the international line refreshing to an 11 August report date lifted headroom by about $17M in one day. Corroboration: Box Office Watch (independent aggregator, fetched 12 August) shows the identical daily ladder and $671.0M domestic / $1.69B worldwide / $1.02B international. Trade press agrees - ScreenDaily headlined '$1.7bn at global box office' and TheWrap reported $1.67B after two weekends, both consistent with a figure that has since ticked up. Box Office Mojo's aggregate figures could not be retrieved directly: its title page (tt22084616) and release page render grosses client-side and returned 'There is no data to display' to the fetch tool. That is a retrieval limitation, not evidence of a discrepancy, and BOM's opening figure of $360,091,572 matches The Numbers exactly where it was retrievable. NO DOWN TRIGGER FIRED. The trigger required both Box Office Mojo AND The Numbers to restate worldwide gross below $1.5B; The Numbers is verified at $1.689B and no restatement of any size was observed on either source in the 11-12 August window. For the question to fail now, a downward restatement of 11.2% would be needed, roughly a hundredfold larger than the largest observed precedent (about 0.11%). Momentum context: the second domestic weekend was $144,254,386, off 60%; Deadline's weekend-three preview (published around 11 August) projects $57M-$72M domestic, down 50-60%. The film sits $311.2M short of $2B, which is now the only live forecasting question.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is 'events that have already physically occurred, where the question asks whether they will occur by a later date'. Worldwide cumulative box office gross is monotonically non-decreasing while a film is in release, and it never goes backwards after release ends. Once a film has crossed a threshold, the only mechanism by which the question can resolve NO is a measurement error - specifically, a downward restatement by the resolving source that pushes the reported figure back below the bar and leaves it there on 31 December 2026. Within box office reporting, the empirical distribution of restatements is tightly concentrated near zero. Sunday-estimate-to-actuals revisions are the largest routine category and typically move totals by a fraction of one percent; the precedent noted in the prior was roughly 0.11% on a $654M domestic base. Larger reclassifications do occur - re-release grosses being split out, territory data being reallocated between studios and aggregators, currency conversion revisions on international lines - but these are typically low single-digit percentages and often move totals upward as late-reporting territories are added. There is no known case where a major film's reported worldwide total was cut by more than 11% after the fact on either Box Office Mojo or The Numbers. Limitations of this reference class: it is thin on genuinely adversarial cases, since the scenario of interest (a large downward restatement) has essentially no observations, so the tail is estimated by reasoning about the reporting process rather than by counting. There is also mild source risk that is not really about the gross at all - a resolving site could go offline, change methodology, or the question could face ambiguity about which source governs if the two diverge. These residual risks justify holding the estimate at 'greater than 99.9%' rather than asserting absolute certainty, but they do not move the rounded central estimate off 100.

forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD at 99%, 80% CI [98,99]. No move. Stating the hold plainly: nothing new on revenue appeared in this window. What DID appear, all dated 11 August 2026: (1) Bloomberg reported Anthropic struck a $9.1B, 20-year lease with Riot Platforms for 191MW of IT capacity at Rockdale, Texas, phased to 96MW by December 2027 and full buildout by June 2028, with two five-year extensions taking the potential total to $16.1B; Riot shares jumped roughly 18-25%. This follows a reported $10B Volta Infra deal and a ~$45B xAI compute purchase in May. (2) Fortune reported Anthropic will embed invisible watermarks in Claude text output under EU AI Act commitments. (3) Anthropic expanded its Compliance API to cover Cowork and Claude Code. (4) OpenAI expanded its Daybreak cybersecurity programme and introduced GPT-5.6-Cyber for vetted defenders. None of these is an ARR disclosure. The compute deal is a weak positive demand signal - a firm does not sign a 20-year, $9.1B power-and-space lease while expecting run-rate contraction - but it is capex, not revenue, and it is given only a fraction of a point. TRIGGER CHECK. DOWN triggers: none fired. No public S-1 from either company appeared on EDGAR as of 12 August; Anthropic's draft was confidentially submitted 1 June 2026 and OpenAI's on 8 June 2026, and coverage still puts OpenAI's public prospectus in the mid-to-late August window with a September roadshow, and Anthropic's roadshow in September ahead of a targeted October Nasdaq listing. No month-over-month ARR decline was reported for either firm. No named outlet published a combined figure below $70B. No product suspension, enforcement action or infrastructure failure hit either firm in the window. UP triggers: none fired either. No named outlet published Q4 2026 figures for both companies; OpenAI was not reported above $70B alone. Standing arithmetic is unchanged: Anthropic's last company disclosure is $47B run-rate (announced with the Series H, closed 28 May 2026), OpenAI's last named-outlet figure is The Information's roughly $25B annualised, reportedly flat since February 2026 at about $2B a month. That sums to roughly $71-72B on disclosures alone, before any H2 growth. Third-party trackers put the pair far higher - TickerTrends had Anthropic at about $74.1B and OpenAI at about $41.3B in July - but trackers do not resolve this question. The unresolved gross-versus-net question on Anthropic's cloud-reseller revenue persists: OpenAI's CRO argued in an April internal memo that Anthropic's then-$30B figure was overstated by about $8B. That dispute did not advance in this window.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: high-growth private technology companies sustaining or exceeding a previously reported annualised run-rate over a four-to-five month forward window. ARR is a run-rate measure, not a trailing accounting figure, and enterprise contracts are predominantly annual with usage-based API layers on top, so month-to-month contraction of the magnitude needed here is rare. Historical base rate for such firms not falling more than 3% below a reported run-rate over five months is well above 95% absent a demand shock, a major restatement, or a product ban. A second and arguably tighter reference class applies: cases where a threshold is already cleared by the LAST reported figures and the question is only whether it holds. Here the disclosed figures already sum to roughly $71-72B with five months of growth still to come, and both companies are in IPO processes that generate disclosure rather than suppress it. Limitations, stated honestly. First, this is a reporting question, not a revenue question. Resolution requires a named outlet or company disclosure to publish Q4 2026 ARR for BOTH firms. That is a coverage-availability risk rather than a fundamentals risk, and it is the single largest remaining source of failure. It is heavily mitigated by two live IPO processes that will force audited public financials, but a delayed or pulled listing could reduce disclosure cadence. Second, the gross-versus-net accounting question on Anthropic's AWS, Google and Microsoft channel revenue is genuinely unresolved; if a public S-1 presents net revenue as the headline and a resolver applies that basis, Anthropic's contribution could fall materially. This is a definitional tail risk, not a growth risk. Third, there is a small ambiguity between quarterly revenue figures (Anthropic's reported roughly $10.9B Q2 2026) and annualised run-rate; conflating them would distort the comparison. Fourth, the reference class contains few observations of companies growing this fast, so the historical base rate may understate both upside and volatility. A ceiling of 99 rather than higher reflects these definitional and reporting risks, not doubt about the underlying revenue.

Barclays put consumer spending at +2%, the strongest of the year, so the household read is mixed rather than clearly weak. Second, gilts round-tripped inside a single session. Trading Economics reported the 10-year yield topping 5% on 11 August (intraday around 5.04%) as Brent passed $89 on Strait of Hormuz tensions, with markets more than fully pricing a BoE hike by December and another by spring; later the same day it fell back below 5% to about 4.95% as Pakistan signalled the US and Iran were close to an arrangement. Neither the >5.5% DOWN trigger nor the <4% UP trigger fired; the level is essentially where the prior left it. Third, and the main reason for the small downgrade, Capital Economics estimated (reported 11 August) that Chancellor John Healey's 28 October Budget could carry up to £25bn of tax rises, roughly 0.8% of GDP, funding about £40bn of commitments and lifting the tax burden to a record ~39% of GDP. Fourth, the Environment Agency reported 71.3% of England in drought after the driest July in 190 years, reservoirs at 69% and over 1,500 abstraction restrictions - a modest but real constraint on the water-intensive data-centre buildout that underpins the AI upside case. NO UP TRIGGER FIRED: no OBR, IMF or OECD revision to UK potential growth (the last relevant marks were the May IMF Article IV and July OECD survey, both already in the prior); no evidence of AI productivity broadening beyond SIC 62/63 since the Bank of England staff work of 6 August; and no positive business-investment surprise against a BCC Q2 reading of only 17% of firms planning to raise capex, a post-pandemic low. The net is a fractionally worse cost-of-capital and fiscal backdrop with no offsetting structural news.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class remains UK decade-average annual real GDP growth: 1990s about 2.2%, 2000s about 1.8%, 2010s about 2.0%, 2020s to date about 1.0% including the pandemic collapse and rebound. Three of the last four completed decades cleared 1.5%, a naive base rate of 60-75%. That number must be discounted heavily. Decades are not independent draws; the post-2008 productivity break is a level-and-slope shift that persists, and the pre-2008 decades were flattered by rapid labour force expansion that will not repeat. The forward-looking decomposition dominates: trend productivity of roughly 1% (the OBR's own medium-term assumption, per its November 2025 productivity briefing paper) plus labour supply growth falling toward 0.5% or less gives potential growth near 1.4-1.5%, right on the threshold. ONS 2024-based projections have natural change turning negative from 2026, with essentially all population growth from migration, and net migration projected to dip to around 138,000 in 2026 before stabilising near 230,000. The IMF's 2026 Article IV put potential growth at 1.4%; the OBR has 1.1% in 2026 then about 1.6% a year thereafter. Because the threshold sits within a few tenths of the central estimate, the answer is close to a coin flip conditional on the potential-growth estimate being right, and the mass below 1.5% is larger because the distribution of shocks over a decade is left-skewed. Limitations: only four prior decades, so the base rate is statistically thin; ONS methodology and Blue Book revisions can move a decade average by 0.1-0.2pp mechanically; a single deep recession in the 2030s costs roughly 0.3-0.5pp on the decade mean; and a genuine AI-driven productivity acceleration is a fat right tail with no historical analogue in this sample.
